section.title: Learn languages that change how you think
section.deck: Roberto Ierusalimschy recommends contrasting language designs as a way to broaden programming judgment.

blocks.question: Which languages should an engineer learn to become a better programmer?
answer: Ierusalimschy starts with Haskell because it exposes the ideas of functional programming in a particularly complete form. He recalls a community joke: C can make an implementation efficient quickly while correctness takes much longer; Haskell can make correctness easier while efficiency becomes the harder task. He treats this as an illustration of differing design priorities, not a performance law. Haskell also shows how pervasive type inference can keep programs statically typed without requiring explicit annotations everywhere.

Next he recommends C, or another low-level language, to understand what a machine actually does. Assembly can serve that purpose, but modern instruction sets are complicated; he suggests that an older, simpler assembler can make the underlying model easier to see. The educational value lies in understanding representation and execution rather than merely learning contemporary syntax.

Scheme is another favorite because a small set of concepts supports surprisingly powerful programs. His answer extends beyond the requested three choices: he also mentions an old pattern-matching language, rendered in the captions as “Snowball,” as an example of a design worth examining. The precise spelling is uncertain in these captions. Older languages can reveal ideas that modern languages copy, omit, or make overly uniform. Even an idea one would not adopt can be useful to understand.
